clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 50s with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented with 1 week of fever, nausea, vomiting, and generalized weakness, progressing to confusion, back pain, urinary hesitancy, and lower extremity numbness/weakness. Physical examination revealed fever (38.9°C), disorientation, upper motor neuron signs (ankle clonus, upgoing toes bilaterally), and 4+/5 strength in lower extremities. Initial MRI brain showed diffuse leptomeningitis with linear radial perivascular enhancement surrounding the lateral ventricles (characteristic of GFAP astrocytopathy, noted retrospectively), while initial MRI spine was normal. CSF demonstrated lymphocytic pleocytosis (WBC 85-501/mm3, 87% lymphocytes), elevated protein (306 mg/dL), and normal glucose. Extensive infectious workup (MTB, HIV, syphilis, fungal, viral PCRs) and preliminary autoimmune screening (AQP4, MOG, oligoclonal bands, ACE) were negative. Due to rapidly progressive course with worsening weakness, repeat spine MRI 11 days later showed longitudinally extensive patchy T2 hyperintense signal throughout the central grey and lateral columns of the cervical and thoracic spine. Meningeal and brain biopsy excluded infectious organisms. Empiric pulse methylprednisolone (1000mg IV daily x 5 days) was initiated, followed by solumedrol 60mg IV daily, resulting in clinical stabilization. CSF subsequently tested positive for GFAP antibodies at 1:128 titer (Mayo Clinic autoimmune encephalitis panel), confirming the diagnosis. Two weeks after the second MRI, the patient demonstrated clinical and radiologic improvement. At 3-month follow-up, he was ambulating with a cane with full strength throughout except 4+/5 hip flexors bilaterally.
